analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and insurers to publish actual prices and creates real penalties for hiding them.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan hospital and insurer price transparency bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force hospitals to post their real prices — including what they negotiated with each insurer and their discounted cash price — in one standard format, and would fine hospitals up to $5 million a year for refusing. It would also require health plans to publish their in-network rates, out-of-network payments, and drug costs every three months in files anyone can download, and to build free tools showing a patient their expected bill before treatment. A federal watchdog would report on whether hospitals and insurers actually comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients deciding on care, uninsured or self-pay patients comparing cash prices, employers shopping for health plans, and researchers studying why care costs what it does. Anyone who has been surprised by a hospital bill would get prices upfront instead of months later.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish, free and in plain language, a list of standard charges for at least 300 'shoppable' services — including the gross charge, the discounted cash price, and the exact rate negotiated with each named insurer [S3].

The bill puts the price disclosure rule into statute and requires CMS to create one standard format so prices are comparable across hospitals, plus regularly check that what hospitals post is accurate [S2].

Hospitals that don't fix noncompliance within 90 days face civil monetary penalties — for larger hospitals, at least $5 million for a full year of violations — and CMS must maintain a public, real-time list of compliant and noncompliant hospitals, naming who got warnings or fines [S3].

Health plans must report every three months their in-network rates, out-of-network payments, and the net amount they pay for each drug (after rebates) in free, machine-readable files, and must run a real-time tool telling patients their expected cost sharing, deductibles met so far, and any prior-authorization or step-therapy requirements [S3].
The Government Accountability Office must report on compliance and enforcement and recommend ways to improve transparency for patients, employers, and the public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which face compliance costs, public shaming on a CMS noncompliance list, and penalties up to $5 million a year; and health insurers, which must open up their negotiated rates and drug payments to public inspection. Insurers would also bear the cost of building the real-time cost-estimate tools.

drawbacks.text: Transparency alone does not guarantee lower bills: patients in emergencies or mid-treatment often cannot shop by price, and researchers have found many people never use the existing price files, so the bill's benefits depend on consumers or employers actually acting on the data [S3].

Hospitals have long argued that publishing every negotiated rate could push some prices up — hospitals with lower rates may use the files to demand more, and the requirement to disclose rates for at least 300 services is a real administrative burden, especially for small rural hospitals, though the bill scales penalties down to $300 a day for hospitals with 30 beds or fewer [S3].
Much of what the bill requires builds on price transparency rules that already existed, so its main additions are enforcement teeth and standardization rather than entirely new disclosure [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but not automatic: knowing prices only saves money if patients, employers, or referees of the market use the information, and emergency care cannot be shopped at all. The costs fall on hospitals and insurers and are mostly one-time compliance work. The strongest version of the bill is its enforcement — most hospital transparency problems since the federal rule took effect have come from lax enforcement, and this bill attacks that directly with a standardized format, audits, named penalties, and a public compliance list.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received any further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Cathy McMorris Rodgers introduced the bill on April 18, 2023 together with Representative Frank Pallone, the top Democrat on the committee it went to, making it bipartisan from the start [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction; that was the last action of any kind in the record [S5].
The bill ended the 118th Congress with a single cosponsor and no committee or floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health insurers are better off: their negotiated rates stay out of easy public view, and no standardized format, public compliance list, or multi-million-dollar penalties will come from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers keep opaque prices

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by the Republican chair of the Energy and Commerce Committee together with the committee's top Democrat, and its one recorded cosponsor was also a Democrat; no vote ever occurred to test opposition.

industries.note: Hospitals would have to publish gross charges, discounted cash prices, and every insurer-specific negotiated rate for at least 300 services in one standard format, and face civil penalties — at least $5 million for a year of ongoing violations at larger hospitals — plus being named on a public CMS noncompliance list. Their interest in keeping negotiated rates out of plain view runs directly against patients' interest in knowing prices in advance.

Plans would have to disclose their in-network rates, out-of-network payments, and net drug payments every three months in publicly downloadable files, and build real-time tools showing members their expected costs and coverage restrictions. Insurers' negotiated rates are central to how they price coverage, and public disclosure removes a competitive advantage that comes at consumers' expense.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug supply intermediaries
industries.note: The bill requires plans to report what they actually pay for each drug net of rebates, discounts, and price concessions, which would expose the spread between list prices and net prices that intermediaries profit from. The disclosure is indirect but touches the core opacity of the drug pricing chain.
